title: What Insulation Is Mold Resistant? Your Options
h1: What Insulation Is Most Mold Resistant?
description: Which insulation resists mold best: how fiberglass, mineral wool, cellulose, spray foam and rigid foam compare, and why moisture control matters most.
quick_answer: Mineral wool and closed-cell spray foam are among the most mold-resistant insulation types, and fiberglass and rigid foam boards don't feed mold on their own. Cellulose is treated to resist mold but can hold water if it gets wet. No insulation is mold-proof, though. Dust and moisture can still grow mold on almost any surface.
body:
Why does insulation get moldy in the first place?

Mold grows where there's moisture and something to feed on. Most modern insulation materials aren't good mold food by themselves, but the dust, debris and paper facing on them can be. When insulation gets wet from a roof leak, a sweating duct or a damp crawl space and stays wet, mold finds a way to grow.

That's why the type of insulation matters less than keeping it dry. The most mold-resistant product will still have problems if it sits in water.

How do common insulation types compare?

Insulation typeMold resistanceNotes
Mineral woolVery goodMade from stone or slag fibers. Doesn't absorb much water and dries out well.
Closed-cell spray foamVery goodResists water and also air seals. Needs professional installation and isn't easily removed later.
Rigid foam boardGoodDoesn't feed mold. Seams need to be sealed or moisture can collect behind it.
Fiberglass batts or blown fiberglassGoodGlass fibers don't feed mold, but paper facings and trapped dust can. Loses performance when wet.
CelluloseFair to goodTreated with borates that resist mold and pests, but it absorbs water and can stay damp if soaked.
Open-cell spray foamFairAir seals well but can absorb water if there's a leak.

Which insulation is best for attics in Southern California?

Most attics here use blown-in fiberglass or cellulose because they cover the attic floor evenly and fill around framing and wiring. Both work well when the attic is dry and well ventilated.

Homes near the coast deal with more humidity and salt air, so good attic ventilation and air sealing matter even more. Inland attics get extremely hot in summer, so depth of insulation is a bigger concern there. In either case, sealing the attic floor and fixing leaky ducts first keeps moist indoor air and condensation out of the insulation.

What about crawl spaces and garages?

Crawl spaces tend to be damp, so moisture-tolerant materials make more sense there. Rigid foam, closed-cell spray foam and mineral wool hold up better than paper-faced batts. A vapor barrier over the soil and good drainage are just as important as the insulation itself.

Walls are a different case. Insulating existing stucco walls usually means blowing material into closed cavities, and any hidden leak in that wall can soak it. If you're opening walls during a remodel, that's the best time to check for past water damage and choose a material that tolerates occasional moisture.

Garages with living space above benefit from insulation that also blocks air, since car exhaust and fumes shouldn't drift into bedrooms.

Does attic ventilation affect mold in insulation?

Yes. A well-vented attic lets moist air escape through soffit and roof vents. When soffit vents get buried under blown-in insulation, painted over or blocked by stored boxes, moisture can build up under the roof deck, especially on cool coastal nights. You may see dark staining on the underside of the roof sheathing first.

Baffles at the eaves keep insulation from blocking soffit vents while still letting you insulate right up to the edge of the attic. Any good insulation job should include them where they're needed.

How do you keep any insulation mold-free?

  • Fix roof leaks and plumbing leaks quickly.
  • Keep soffit and roof vents clear so the attic can breathe.
  • Make sure bathroom and kitchen fans vent outside, not into the attic.
  • Seal and insulate attic ducts so they don't sweat.
  • Keep the AC condensate drain clear.
  • Remove insulation that's been soaked, moldy or contaminated by rodents rather than covering it.

Should moldy insulation be replaced?

Yes. Insulation that has grown mold, been soaked or been fouled by rodents doesn't insulate well and can keep releasing odors and spores. It should be removed, the moisture source fixed, the area cleaned, and fresh insulation installed.

Our attic insulation team handles removal of damaged insulation, attic cleanup, air sealing and new insulation, so the new material goes into a clean, dry space.
faqs: The glass fibers themselves don't feed mold, so fiberglass is fairly resistant. Mold can still grow on dust trapped in it or on paper facings, especially if the insulation gets wet. Kept dry, fiberglass rarely has mold problems.

Cellulose is treated with borates that help resist mold and pests. It absorbs water, though, so if a roof leak soaks it, it can stay damp long enough for mold to grow and it may settle and lose effectiveness. Wet cellulose usually needs to be replaced.
Is spray foam the best choice to prevent mold?

Closed-cell spray foam resists water and air seals, which helps a lot. It isn't the right answer for every attic, though, and it's harder to remove or inspect behind later. Good air sealing, ventilation and moisture control prevent mold with almost any insulation type.
How can I tell if my attic insulation has mold?

Look for dark spots or discoloration on the insulation, the roof sheathing or the framing, and notice any musty smell in the attic or upstairs rooms. Clumped or matted insulation and water stains are warning signs too. A professional inspection can confirm it.
